full_text:
Hey! Scott Barrett here.

As I’m working through my rankings for my Draft Guide (which should be out August 3rd), the trickiest thing for me to get right is always injuries — injury risk, injury discounts, estimated timelines to return, timelines to return to full 100% effectiveness, etc. — because I’m not a Doctor.

Luckily, Jeff Mueller *is* a doctor, and he also happens to be the best injury expert in the fantasy space (by far). So, I asked him to come work for Fantasy Points. And for his first article, I told him to answer all of the top, burning questions I had come up with while working through my rankings. You can find our Q&A below. And for those of you who hate reading, Jeff and I have both provided a TL;DR (too long; didn’t read) section for you.

__Who are you? What’s your background? Why should we take your recommendations seriously?__

My name is Jeff Mueller, a Doctor of Physical Therapy for 11 years in an outpatient orthopedic physical therapy clinic with an emphasis on sports rehab. I have worked with a vast number of high school and college athletes, as well as a handful of current and former professional athletes, including MLB and NFL players, D1 college athletes in baseball, softball, football, wrestling, and swimming, and even an extreme athlete through Cirque Du Soleil.

While all of that sounds great and the experience certainly helps in my content creation for projection of athletic return, my recommendations should be taken seriously due to the immense amount of studying and learning that I have done over the years. I love fantasy football, and I work hard in producing content that is not biased and remains objective throughout the entire process. Your money is at stake, and I do not take that lightly with my recommendations on injury projections.

__I have a gigantic man crush on Cam Skattebo, who averaged 19.3 FPG across the six games he played at least a dozen snaps last year. How worried should we be about Skattebo’s health coming off such a gruesome injury (dislocated ankle, fibula fracture, ruptured deltoid ligament)? Will he be ready by Week 1? Should we expect 100% full effectiveness when he does return? Or is this like a 2025 Chris Godwin situation? For what it’s worth,__ [__it seems__](https://x.com/SleeperNFL/status/2057116742825238723?s=20) __Giants brass is very bullish, fully expecting him to be their bell cow RB this season.__

Skattebo’s injury was significantly worse than Quinshon Judkins’ injury in terms of overall damage and tissue trauma that occurred. First off, one of the concerns many have brought up is that his injury was an open wound, meaning the bone pierced through the skin. The primary concern with an open wound is a heightened risk of infection early in the recovery process, so the fact that he did not develop an infection is a great sign. The open wound portion of the injury does not guarantee that the bone break was more significant than past incidents for other players; it simply means that the bone broke and punctured the skin.

Once the early recovery process is in the rearview mirror, that open-wound risk can essentially be forgotten, shifting the remaining risk towards the severity of ligament damage when projecting his 2026 season production. I would say this scenario is closer to a Tony Pollard 2023 type of scenario than a Chris Godwin two-surgery complication 2025 scenario, with one key negative being that Skattebo suffered a tibia fracture alongside a deltoid ligament rupture, while Pollard suffered only a fibula fracture with ligament damage. However, Pollard was active for Week 1 in under 8 months post-operatively, while Skattebo will be 10.5 months post-operative by the time Week 1 comes around.

Pollard wound up rushing for over 1,000 yards coming off of his ankle fracture and dislocation with decent numbers within his first three games: 4.8% explosive run rate, 53.2% success rate, 0.11 missed tackles forced, and 2.56 YACO/A per Fantasy Points Data. From Weeks 4-6 prior to their Week 7 bye, he displayed a 39% drop in explosive run percentage, a 23% drop in success rate, a similar MTF rate, and a 14% drop in YACO/A. From weeks 8-17, Pollard wound up finishing strong with a 5.0% explosive run rate, 48.2% success rate, 0.17 MTF, and 2.69 YACO/A, displaying positive improvements coming out of his bye week in his featured role. All of this to say as we look into Pollard’s 2023 season split up into sections, I will not be surprised if we witness a similar trajectory for Skattebo with a solid start to the 2026 season with a possible dip after the first 3-4 weeks in per-touch efficiency due to conditioning and recovery struggles early on, and then a strong return after the Week 8 bye through the remainder of the season.

I anticipate Skattebo being active Week 1 and hitting the ground running initially, but his body slowly recovering compared to normal as he gets back into live game reps, leading to a mini-dip in efficiency pre-bye week that should improve post-bye week. One other variable that I find difficult to assign an objective measure to is the mental component of return to play, which many players struggle with and manifests as movement hesitation once they return to actual live game repetitions. I do not think Skattebo will struggle with this — the guy is already doing backflips, you might have heard. It is another piece of the puzzle that tells me that once Skattebo hits the field, he is not going to be fearful or hesitant to run through a mess of players and smash a linebacker’s face in.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Stop panicking about Cam Skattebo doing backflips. He is clearly comfortable performing risky movements, which is fantastic at this rate for the mental component of returning from a significant injury. I would prefer that players be confident in being themselves rather than cowering over potential reinjury. This team will be run heavy with Skattebo leading the backfield. Invest despite the anticipated first-quarter production dip.

__Scott's Takeaway:__ Jeff's write-up makes me much more comfortable drafting Skattebo. The Tony Pollard comparison is especially encouraging — Pollard's first year back felt disappointing, but only because he was being drafted in Round 2 after a career season. Skattebo is already being discounted into Rounds 4-5, which feels much more than fair. I'm viewing him as a high-end to mid-range RB2, which means his RB21 price tag on Sleeper is way too low.

__How worried should I be about Alec Pierce, coming off ankle surgery? Is there any chance he misses Week 1? How much of training camp is he going to miss? Does__ [__his leg look atrophied__](https://x.com/RomeovilleKid/status/2059693649911333118?s=20) __to you? How much of a concern is this for a player who primarily wins on speed? After getting paid top-12 WR money, he’s supposed to magically morph into being a true alpha WR1 (less of the deep threat-only type he’s been, more of PPR cheat code with a shallow, more horizontal route tree) this year? Does that seem likely to you?__

Based on video of Pierce walking around OTAs, my speculation is that he had an arthroscopic debridement or cleanup of his talus, the main weight-bearing bone in the ankle joint. On video shot approximately three months post-operatively, he was still struggling to step through over his talus. Considering he is required to sprint at full speed through full ankle range, it is concerning that he was struggling to simply walk with only 3.5 months to go until Week 1, but that does not mean he will not be ready. In fact, recent reports indicate that the hope is that Pierce is ready at some point during training camp or at the start of the preseason.

My concern with Pierce is explosiveness and effectiveness on vertical routes as well as sharp change-of-direction routes. While I do believe there is a good chance he is ready to play Week 1, I anticipate movement deficiencies through November, which will negatively impact his first quarter to half of his 2026 season. If his role does change to more horizontal utilization, I would hope that any in-breaking routes come when he is lined up on the right side of the field rather than the left, so that he does not have to cut sharply and push off his left ankle. After-catch efficiency would still likely be negatively impacted, though.

The other issue is that we have yet to see Pierce used in this fashion, so I remain skeptical that he will be highly effective outside his vertical specialization, which has led to two dings on his profile so far. Unfortunately for Pierce, a third ding comes in the form of Daniel Jones coming off of a right Achilles repair as a right-handed thrower. I anticipate vertical and deep throws being less accurate with less velocity through his first half of the season. If Jones is effective and accurate in the first half of 2026, I anticipate it being on short yardage and across the middle of the field rather than deep downfield or outside the hashes.

If you are hoping for decent production from Pierce to start the season, pray that his role truly does change. Otherwise, like I will be doing, invest heavily in Tyler Warren and consider Josh Downs as a target barring the Colts adding a veteran receiver such as Keenan Allen or Deebo Samuel. As a final note, if the Colts do add a key veteran receiver and news drops that Pierce will not be ready during camp or preseason, my concern for Pierce’s 2026 season grows.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: I am concerned about Alec Pierce for the first half of the season due to anticipated regression in explosiveness and acceleration, and Daniel Jones coming off a right Achilles repair. These two factors place a high risk of their vertical connection being disrupted until they both improve health-wise closer to midseason. I will continue to invest heavily in Tyler Warren for this pass attack.

__Scott's Takeaway:__ This is enough for me to move Pierce below consensus. Between the ankle concerns, the leap of faith required around his new role, and Daniel Jones recovering from an Achilles tear, there are just too many hurdles to clear. Meanwhile, Josh Downs continues to look like one of my favorite values at the position.

__Kenneth Walker missed six games in 2024 and was (seemingly) load-managed for the entire 2025 regular season. Based on all of my angry DMs from November, I’d guess he would be going in Round 10 had the playoffs not happened. Now he’s going Round 2, and no one seems to worry about his “injury risk.” Is that right?__

{{PAYWALL}}

That appears to be correct, with a clear assumption that Walker will all of a sudden be utilized in the way that we all had hoped coming out of college. Oddly enough, I agree with them while factoring in that Andy Reid was once the running back whisperer and Eric Bieniemy gets the best production out of his running backs. With explosive plays and a projected receiving workload, I could see a scenario in which Walker outscores fan-favorite Omarion Hampton, justifying the Round 2 cost.

Outside of 2024, Walker has played at least 15 games in every season, including all 20 games last season. We have seen him produce 18+ FPG while playing anywhere from 40-65% snaps, so I do believe the Chiefs can “load-manage” him while getting the absolutely most out of every single touch that he does receive. While Walker carries a bit more injury risk than other running backs in his range due to past lower body injuries, I am still bullish on him at cost, considering players after him such as Nico Collins, Chris Olave, AJ Brown, Tee Higgins and more have just as much injury concern going into 2026.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Arguably the best and most explosive running back that the RB whisperers Andy Reid and Eric Bieniemy have had in Kansas City since Kareem Hunt in 2017, I am eagerly investing at cost despite the past injury concerns. I am willing to look past the prior soft tissue injuries given the upside, particularly when the players around him at cost also have past soft tissue injuries.

__Scott's Takeaway:__ I agree with Jeff’s assessment that Walker’s injury history almost feels like a moot point, given how much Kansas City paid him, all of the comments from the coaching staff this offseason, and given the lack of talent behind Walker on the depth chart. Honestly, it feels like Walker’s median projection should be 2017 Kareem Hunt barring injury, which means — if the injury risk is as negligible as Jeff is making it out to be — Walker is a good-to-great pick at current ADP (RB12-14).

__Any concern with Bo Nix and his ankle injury/surgery, especially considering it's the same ankle with multiple injuries since college?__

My primary concern with Nix is that he has had four surgeries on his right ankle since high school, with the most recent requiring two surgeries. The good news is that Dr. Norman Waldrop performed the most recent surgeries, so we know that the quality of work is pristine. He has already been running around and throwing with plans to be a full go for training camp, which fits the timeframe for his second surgery in late April. I do believe that he can have a very solid 2026 season, but rushing production and longevity are my primary concerns for Nix for 2026 and dynasty.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Despite an anticipated rushing production dip due to two more ankle surgeries, the addition of Jaylen Waddle has me intrigued about investing in Nix for the 2026 season. He has already produced very well in the past few seasons with inconsistent offensive weapons, so I lean towards not avoiding despite the reinjury risk after the Broncos boosted the attack.

__Scott's Takeaway:__ This reinforces why I'm lower on Nix than consensus. Even if he's healthy enough to start Week 1, I think the rushing upside — which is a huge part of any QB’s fantasy appeal — takes a step back this season. At his current price, I'd rather chase quarterbacks with higher ceilings.

__Is Joe Burrow injury-prone?__

If you play in the NFL and you get hit a lot, you are probably prone to injury. Until Burrow can consistently get the ball out of his hands faster, rather than holding onto it and taking as many sacks as he does, I will maintain that he is injury-prone. I do not have a specific concern about reinjury risk from one of his previous injuries, but more so his playstyle and how many sacks he takes.

Every year, people talk about concerns with mobile quarterbacks, but the concerns with a pocket passer lead to an equal risk of injury, as defenders or offensive linemen roll up on a quarterback's ankle or knee from any angle.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Yes, Burrow is injury-prone mostly due to how long he holds the ball, leading to a high number of sacks and risk of defenders or his offensive linem4n rolling up on his ankles and knees. I would still draft him without hesitation, given his projected pass volume and surrounding weapons.

__Scott's Takeaway:__ The biggest takeaway for me isn't Burrow — it's Ja'Marr Chase. Even if Burrow *were* much more likely than any other QB to miss time, Cincinnati now has one of the league's better backup QBs in Joe Flacco. Chase averaged 21.5 fantasy points per game with Flacco last year, so I'm not downgrading him at all.

__If Malik Nabers were 100% fully healthy, I’d be drafting him in Round 1. Do you think he’ll be ready by Week 1? And at what point should we expect him to be back to 100% effectiveness?__

Malik Nabers had an ACL reconstruction plus meniscus repair at the bare minimum, with likely more damage addressed that we may never know about. He had remained on crutches with his Bledsoe brace through 11-12 weeks post-operative, which is well beyond the standard six weeks and our first sign that he was behind schedule in a typical protocol. He then required a second surgery to remove a cyclops lesion — scar tissue that developed on his ACL graft and was restricting his full knee extension and flexion range of motion — in May.

The team announced that the second surgery would not extend his timeframe for recovery, but I would argue that his limitations due to the scar tissue set him back by several months, with the second surgery restarting a small inflammatory process that likely adds close to an extra month. Despite that thought process about the scar tissue, [it appears](https://x.com/JordanRaanan/status/2080410075458371805?s=20) that Nabers will avoid starting training camp on PUP, which will allow him to begin practicing with the team immediately. As of right now, I still think it is 50/50 whether Nabers will be ready for Week 1, but it is fantastic news that he will not begin on PUP. (There have been several players who have also avoided PUP for training camp but then wound up still missing Weeks 1-2 of the NFL season before making their season debut — see Chris Godwin last year.)

Either way, we should obviously view this as a big positive for Nabers because the sooner he can get practice repetitions in and the sooner he can hit the NFL field in live-game repetitions, the sooner his production dip can return to normal. The next big question is when we will see him reach 100% effectiveness, which would be easier to answer once we know when he will debut. If he is active Week 1, then it may only take the first quarter of the season for him to reach full effectiveness. If he is not active until Week 3 or 4, then it may be closer to Week 8 or 9 when we see him reach full effectiveness.

Initially, I was recommending avoiding Nabers in Round 3 with a preference that he drops into the Round 4 range, but with this news that he will avoid PUP for training camp with a chance to be active in Week 1 (or at least earlier than we thought), I am now okay drafting him in Round 3. Be cautious, though, as managers prop him up too high into Round 2, as he will still be coming off of a significant ACL plus meniscus repair surgery that typically leads to a production dip of 10-20% in the total Year 1 out of surgery.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: The great news is that Malik Nabers will be avoiding PUP to begin training camp. I do not fully know whether this means he is ready to practice with the team, or if this is a procedural step to allow Nabers to be around the team (as in the Chris Godwin situation last year). We will find out soon whether he is participating in padded drills and whether he truly has a chance to be active in Week 1, or if he is still slowly ramping up and winds up missing a handful of games. The sooner he practices, the better, and the sooner he hits the NFL field, the better, with regard to seeing his production steadily ramp up to near full effectiveness. If he is active Week 1, he will likely pay off at Round 3 prices by Week 5 or soon after. I am now less nervous to draft him for 2026.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ Given how underwhelming Chris Godwin’s 2024 was, this write-up was a lot more optimistic than I was expecting it to be. The question I need to answer now is, “Is Malik Nabers a player we want to draft? Or a player we merely want to buy-low on in September or October?”

__I’ve always joked that George Kittle is like if Mr. Glass, Wolverine, and The Juggernaut were all the same superhero. Because he’s always hurt, but also always beating timelines and__ [__playing through a million different injuries to great success__](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1914708032665112924?s=20)__. Any chance he can be on the field for the 49ers in Week 1? At what point should we expect him back to 100% full effectiveness?__

If the 49ers' Week 1 game were in the United States, I would say there's a 90-95% chance of being active against the Rams. However, considering the extensive travel time to Australia and that Kittle’s rest and recovery regimen will be disrupted by unfamiliar facilities, my sense is that he will be inactive for Week 1 and debut in Week 2 of the 2026 season.

Video from TEU showed that he is still hesitant to fully push off and accelerate from his right leg — that would put his Achilles in an extended position similar to how it ruptured. Regarding 100% effectiveness, we may not see that until closer to mid-season, given the risk that the 49ers do not need to lean on him offensively as usual with the addition of Mike Evans and the presumed health of Ricky Pearsall. I anticipate more of a boom-bust nature for production for Kittle’s 2026 season.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: I expect Kittle to be active either Week 1 or Week 2 (due to travel to Australia), with more of a boom/bust weekly production coming off of the Achilles repair and addition of Mike Evans. Explosiveness within his routes and with the ball in his hands likely improves closer to 85-90% by midseason.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ To me, this means George Kittle represents an extreme value as the ADP TE11 on Yahoo! and Sleeper. You can pair a cheaper Isaiah Likely or Dallas Goedert with Kittle, and then that combination (Likely/Goedert in the first half, Kittle in the second half) will almost assuredly outscore a number of TEs being drafted ahead of Kittle.

__When should we expect Zach Charbonnet back, and in what form? Is there a chance he sits out all of 2026?__

Based on how he was moving in video seen in June, I do not believe that he will miss all of 2026. The safe return on paper remains in late November once he has reached 9 months post-operative; however, recent research has shown that an athlete can return safely as long as they meet all key milestones and measures as early as 7.5 to 8 months post-operatively. With this in mind, I believe the soonest we see Charbonnet play is mid- to late-October.

The sooner he returns to the field, the sooner his production ramp-up can begin. If he is active in October, I believe he could pay off as a weekly starter if he retains the goal-line role but would likely be heavily reliant on touchdowns. If he is active in October, I believe his ramp-up to fantasy viability on a weekly basis would increase up until late November. If he is not active until November, he would be a risky start through December, especially if Jadarian Price is performing well before Charbonnet returns.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Anticipate a November return for Charbonnet with a slow ramp-up into December, while Jadarian Price is the most likely to work his way into a substantial workload until Charbonnet is cleared for return to play. Price’s upside may be nerfed come fantasy playoffs.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ This has me very bullish on Price. It seems there’s a very good chance he’s already established himself as “the guy” by the time Charbonnet returns to ~90% effectiveness in December. And up until that point, his primary competition is George Holani and his 28 career NFL touches.

__Last year, Davante Adams averaged 17.1 FPG (~WR6) across the 12 games he played on at least 49% of the team’s snaps. But he also missed multiple games with knee and hamstring injuries. How much should we be worried about him in his age-33 season?__

These next few sentences will hold true for several cases that you can think of, including the next topic after this question. Hamstring strains often do not heal to a 100% pre-injury state, particularly as you age. Scar tissue and minor structural remodeling commonly occur, leading to less-than-100% healing and leaving the athlete prone to reinjury in the same fibers that were previously injured.

Athletes heal better in their young 20s and into mid-20s, and do not heal as well in their 30s. Thus, we should be concerned about the state of soft tissue health in players like Adams. I believe that the Rams, who have one of the best sports science and rehabilitation resources in the NFL, are aware of this fact and one of the key reasons why they considered trading Adams away while pursuing adding another high-end wide receiver (in this scenario, they were rumored to be pursuing AJ Brown up until they had their own medical concerns on Brown’s knee).

For a player who was highly dependent on touchdowns for weekly fantasy production last season, we should be concerned about the state of Adams’ soft tissue health for 2026.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Adams’ touchdown upside should remain within the Rams offense, but we should be concerned about touchdown regression from Matt Stafford as well as persistent hamstring reinjury of his past strains. Due to a higher reliance on touchdowns versus yardage, I would prefer Adams in Best Ball instead of redraft leagues.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ Adams is definitely not the player he once was (bottom-3 in YAC/R in 2025), but his separation abilities are still there (1st in ASS). Even after accounting for the age and injury concerns, ADP WR20-23 feels like a solid value.

__I think Ryan Heath put it perfectly when he said: “Whatever happens with Mike Evans this year, it will feel incredibly obvious in hindsight. Either he scores a million touchdowns for Kyle Shanahan, or his hamstring falls off the bone like Texas BBQ from practicing next to a haunted 5G Chernobyl super-EMF electrical substation.” How risky is Evans, who is 32-years-old and missed 3+ games with hamstring injuries in back-to-back years?__

What I wrote about Adams fits Mike Evans perfectly, unfortunately. I would argue there is probably more risk for Evans than for Adams due to his nature and style as a long strider, which creates a higher risk of future hamstring strains from muscle lengthening and high deceleration forces during those long strides. It will be a major concern for me to monitor throughout the 2026 season, but if Evans can avoid future strains, his upside is immense in Kyle Shanahan’s offense, particularly as one of the main red-zone threats.

In terms of projected yardage and touchdowns, I would be willing to bet on Evans slightly more than betting on Adams, but by season end I could see this decision being a true coin flip on upside.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: While his playstyle as a long strider gives me concern about reinjury to his past hamstring strains, he finds himself in a tremendous upside situation as the X for Kyle Shanahan’s offense. Invest and hope that the substation curse does not hit him.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ Evans’ age and hamstring history aren’t ideal, but he still feels like an incredible value at his WR26-30 ADP. Like Adams, it helps that the separation abilities are still there — Evans has finished top-3 in ASS in each of the last three seasons — except he’s (inexplicably) much cheaper than Adams.

__Emeka Egbuka averaged 20.5 FPG through the first five weeks of the season, and then picked up a hamstring injury in Week 6, and then, by the end of the season, was splitting WR3 duties 50/50 with Jalen McMillan. What went wrong? Could this injury explain the entirety of Egbuka’s disappointing second half? Or, perhaps, how much is Baker Mayfield to blame? Mayfield was on the practice report listed with an injury 11 times last year, with foot, toe, biceps, knee, oblique, illness, shoulder (left), and shoulder (right) injuries. From Weeks 1-6, Mayfield ranked top-10 in catchable target rate, averaging 19.4 FPG. From Week 7-on, he averaged just 15.5 FPG, and only Shedeur Sanders was worse by CPOE.__

I am relying on some external analysis on this one, but I do believe Egbuka’s struggles can be tied to a mixture of things — being falsely typecasted as an X, his own efficiency concerns coming off of the hamstring strain very early versus letting it heal, Baker Mayfield dealing with eight different injuries (as he revealed on Netflix’s *Quarterback*), and the full wide receiver group getting healthy as the season continued.

Early reports indicate that Egbuka will be utilized heavily in a Cooper Kupp-type role, with heavy movement and as a key target, with Evans now gone and Baker healthy for as long as possible. We saw the production during optimal windows in those first five weeks of his rookie season, so I am willing to bet on him at cost, with even better projections for his utilization in 2026. My main hope moving forward is that, if any of these Tampa Bay players suffer injuries, I would love to see the medical staff keep them out long enough to heal to 100% without playing through injury and production dips.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Knowing that Egbuka produced incredibly well pre-injury and that his second half was impacted by both his own hamstring and Baker’s eight injuries during the season, along with a projected improved utilization with the new offensive coordinator, I am drafting Egbuka heavily for 2026.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ I think I agree with Jeff’s assessment that we can almost write off Egbuka’s Weeks 6-18 in its entirety due to injury. In which case, it’s clear he offers massive league-winning upside at his late-Round 4 / early-Round 5 price tag. For some reason, he’s still a player I’m hesitant to go all-in on, but consider me definitely more bullish on Egbuka than not.

__There’s no chance Chris Godwin steps onto the field in Week 1 and looks exactly as good as he did in 2024 (when he finished behind only Ja’Marr Chase in FPG), right? He’s 30 years old, and looked awful last year, coming off surgery to fix a dislocated ankle. Is the new Chris Godwin the one we saw in 2025, or…__

From Weeks 10 to 18 in 2025, Chris Godwin was WR33 with 1.76 YPRR, WR5 with 7.00 YAC/R, WR9 with 2.56 YACO/R, WR3 with 0.30 MTF/R, and WR23 with 0.103 1D/RR amongst wide receivers who ran a minimum of 100 routes and had a minimum of 15 receptions in those nine weeks (*Fantasy Points Data*). I would not say Godwin looked awful during that time span, coming off a significant ankle injury that required two surgeries and caused complications through August.

Now, with Mike Evans gone and Egbuka expected to play out wide, Godwin should retain his slot role where he has dominated in years past and remain a top target for Baker Mayfield. At cost, I am actually investing in him for the 2026 season with a chance of being a very consistent slot option at wide receiver, though I am not anticipating him returning to his 2024 form when he earned 0.28 TPRR and 2.62 YPRR. He was on par with his YACO/R and MTF/R numbers in the second half of 2025, but I would anticipate him being able to perform somewhere in the middle of his 2025 and 2024 numbers in targets and yards per route run at his age of 30 with the long-desired slot role.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: While I am not anticipating Godwin to match his 2024 numbers, I do anticipate positive growth in his second-half 2025 numbers, further out from his two ankle surgeries, with no Mike Evans present and a strong rapport with a healthy Baker Mayfield. I am drafting at cost despite the age and past injury concerns.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ I’ll be honest, I was expecting a much more pessimistic write-up from Jeff here. Godwin’s probably no longer offers league-winning upside at this stage of his career, but he’s still a decent-to-good value at his current WR38-41 ADP.

__How worried should I be about Chris Olave’s concussion history and/or blood clots?__

Thankfully, neuroplasticity occurs and tells us that the brain can heal without heightened reinjury or recurrent concussion risk. I view Olave in the same light that I once viewed Brandin Cooks: invest and hope that no other concussion occurs. My primary concern regarding Olave’s 2026 production is the pulmonary embolism he is recovering from. The clot has been treated, and it sounds like he is close to being fully cleared for football activity soon, once he is off of blood thinners.

My concern is not if the clot returns, but how his current conditioning level is and how much training he has been able to perform while on blood thinners. Reports seem to indicate that he has been able to train to some capacity, but the main issue after dealing with a lung blood clot is regaining your VO2 max. It can be common to have The concern with Rome Odunze should not be with the specific fracture he suffered. The concern remains with how his “new structure” of how his bone healed will impact his movement system. The displacement of the foot results in altered lower extremity motion/biomechanics.… https://t.co/9J1IIXbPB7 — Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT (@jmthrivept) July 17, 2026 

Is it a guarantee that this happens? No, but definitely a risk that I am not willing to bet on at cost for Odunze considering what he has told the media about his “new normal” and how head coach Ben Johnson has been talking about Luther Burden and Colston Loveland. While I am personally not investing in Odunze because of the structural discussions, I also understand the perspective that if he were to have zero complications within 2026, he is the cheapest of the Chicago passing attack and could wind up paying off due to cost if he winds up performing at even 85-90% of his Weeks 1-5 last season.

While I would exercise caution from a biomechanical standpoint, I have to be honest that I can't predict how this is going to play out for Odunze. We could hope for a return to his Week 1-5 production; however, at that time he was contending with DJ Moore and Cole Kmet for targets, while both Colston Loveland and Luther Burden were at only 38% and 22% route percentages, respectively. When those two players increased to 63% and 43% route percentage within Weeks 8-13, Odunze’s advanced metrics in YPRR, YAC/R, YACO/R, MTF/R, and 1D/RR all dropped below both of Loveland’s and Burden’s. Yes, Odunze was dealing with a stress fracture at the time, but the handpicked rookies, who both missed time in training camp due to injuries, began to grasp the playbook at a higher level and earn more touches and playing time.

I do believe that Odunze will hold a more volatile role in the offense as the out-wide vertical threat where Caleb Williams tends to be less accurate, leading to a more boom/bust season on a weekly basis, while Loveland and Burden take over the YAC and across-the-middle roles that are key for Ben Johnson’s offense.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: I am concerned about Rome Odunze’s “new normal” due to potential biomechanical changes and the risk of future compensatory injuries. Even if he is able to perform at 90% of what he was in Weeks 1-5 of 2025, he will be contending with 75-80%+ route percentages from Colston Loveland and Luther Burden instead of their 20-40%, and will likely still maintain his boom/bust vertical role where Caleb Williams is least accurate. If there are any athleticism dips that could occur from a new structure in the foot, I would bet they come from regression in burst and acceleration, which could limit his explosiveness downfield on vertical routes. Proceed with caution on Odunze.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ This only strengthens my conviction. I'm fading Odunze almost entirely this season, while Luther Burden has become one of my favorite breakout bets in the middle rounds.

__Is Tucker Kraft going to be 100% (back to pre-injury explosiveness) by Week 1?__

By Week 1, I doubt he will be at 100%, but I do believe there is a chance he can be close to 80-85% of his pre-injury explosiveness. He will be very close to 10 months post-operative by Week 1, so I would anticipate him being closer to 100% within November to December.

Again, *this does not mean he cannot be effective in his routes or with the ball in his hands*. I do think people get a little too hung up on not wanting to invest in someone until they are truly 100%, but at cost, I would not hesitate to invest in Kraft for his 2026 production within the Packers system, with Dontayvion Wicks and Romeo Doubs gone. If any regression occurs, I would anticipate it in explosiveness and YAC/R in the first quarter of the season, with a steady increase in efficiency into midseason. It may not lead to top-5 production right off the bat, but he should be able to produce top-12 right away with high upside by midseason, so I am investing.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: I anticipate slight regression in advanced metrics in the first quarter of the season, with a steady ramp-up through midseason. Even with the efficiency dip, Kraft can post top-12 numbers starting in Week 1. Keep investing for 2026 at cost.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ It feels like I can just repeat the same thing about Kittle here in this section. Kraft feels like a terrific value, especially on ESPN (ADP: TE11). Just make sure you’re pairing him with Isaiah Likely (should benefit early in the year from Malik Nabers being less than 100%) or Dallas Goedert (great early-season strength of schedule), just in case Kraft is sluggish out of the gates due to injury.

__The way fantasy analysts talk about Christian McCaffrey, it’s as though drafting him were like you’re flipping a coin — if heads, McCaffrey stays healthy and finishes as top-2 at the position in total fantasy points. If tails, McCaffrey gets hurt and now you have to try to win your league without your Round 1 pick. Is that right? Is that a fair assessment?__

That is a very fair assessment, despite McCaffrey’s incredible training regimen and the many resources he uses to stay healthy. I do believe the 49ers intend to decrease his overall volume, but ultimately it comes down to McCaffrey pulling himself off the field at times and Kyle Shanahan being okay with that.

Even if his volume decreases to some extent, I do anticipate him being on the field in key situations, such as third-down and red-zone opportunities. I also do believe that his receiving workload will reduce, ultimately depending on the health of Mike Evans, Ricky Pearsall, Christian Kirk, and George Kittle. Every single one of those players can be viewed as injury-prone, though, so it is very possible that the 49ers wind up with a depleted depth chart once again and wind up relying on 7 receptions a game from McCaffrey by midseason.

This will be fun to revisit in January, and I wish you the best of luck.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: History tells us that the vast number of touches McCaffrey had last year poses significant risk heading into 2026, with another negative signal being his regression in several advanced metrics as a rusher. Coin flip on drafting for 2026, but if he is healthy, then he will absolutely receive the high-value touches we are drafting him for, including third-down conversions and touchdowns.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ McCaffrey should go no later than RB3 in drafts. Even if he carries more risk than any other Round 1 pick, the upside is immense. And as we all know from Upside Wins Championships, upside is more valuable than downside is detrimental.

__If Chris Rodriguez did, in fact, suffer a Jones fracture, how debilitating might that be for his performance this season? Might it affect his 2026 workload?__

If a running back returns from a Jones fracture repair after 12 weeks post-operatively, the production dip is still fairly low, within a 10-20% range. The further out they are from surgery, the lower the dip. We still do not have concrete intel on specific injury or date of surgery, but just say the surgery was in the first week of May (and I’m fairly certain it was well before this); Week 1 would mark 18 weeks post-operative.

Rodriguez’s status for training camp will give us more information, but I do anticipate him being active in Week 1 with minimal production and efficiency dip this far out from surgery. If the injury were more severe, such as a Lisfranc repair, I would anticipate him starting camp on PUP and remaining on PUP through possibly October or November. We should have more insight soon, but as of now, I anticipate he will be there for camp.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Do not anticipate much of a production dip for Rodriguez coming off of the speculated Jones fracture due to the timeframe from surgery to Week 1, but monitor for more intel that may confirm or give us new details about his exact injury.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ Just keep an eye on news out of Jacksonville’s camp in August. If Rodriguez is slow to get on the field or doesn’t look great, I’ll need to move Bhayshul Tuten way up in my rankings. But right now I’m still projecting 8-12 carries per game for Rodriguez.

__I already know Drake London is an injury discount, but how much so? London started off the season with an AC sprain (suffered in Week 1) and ended the year fighting through a PCL injury (suffered in Week 11). But London was looking like a major league-winner up until that injury. Up until his first missed game from the PCL injury (Week 12), London was averaging 10.5 targets per game (~WR2) on a 33.0% target share (~WR1), 108.5 YPG (~WR1), and 24.5 FPG (~WR1) over his previous six games, hitting 100-plus yards in 5 of those 6 games.__

I do believe that Drake London’s cost assumes similar utilization into the 2026 season despite a new head coach, new offensive coordinator, and new quarterback. I do think the risk of scheme change cancels out the potential injury discount, but he is incredibly intriguing considering Tua Tagovailoa can operate Kevin Stefanski’s scheme with high-level accuracy at a decent rate.

The good news is that PCL sprains have an incredibly low year-to-year recurrence risk, so, at cost, I suppose you can consider London an injury discount. A difficult factor of injury that we may never know, or may not find out until much later, is if his PCL ever truly healed or if this winds up causing complications such as a Dalton Kincaid situation. By all accounts, I have to believe that London’s PCL did heal and is not giving him issues throughout his off-season training. With that in mind, even if he produces at 80-85% of his pre-injury form from weeks 1-11, he was looking at a 30.3% target rate, 0.32 TPRR, 2.90 YPRR, 3.95 YAC/R, a ridiculous 66.7% team touchdown percentage, and a very respectable 0.140 1D/RR prior to suffering the PCL sprain. He has room to regress while still paying off at current cost in drafts.

Based on reports, I believe that we will see a 100% Drake London in 2026, and you should draft him accordingly.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: While there is always an unknown risk that some of these players may not fully heal from their injuries, all accounts indicate that the PCL sprain is no longer an issue for London. Even if he regresses a small amount from his advanced metrics in 2025, which I believe we will see a 100% return to form, I am not hesitating to draft London at cost.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ If London had never suffered the PCL injury, I think we'd be drafting him in Round 1. Instead, we get him a round or two later despite every indication that he’s now fully healthy. As it stands, he’s the Round 2-4 WR I expect to have the most exposure to this year.

__How worried should redraft managers be about A.J. Brown? How worried should dynasty managers be? Why?__

I believe Brown’s knee is a ticking time bomb, but there is no way to know whether that is 2026 or later, which makes injury projection difficult. We do know that his knee is degenerative, so there is risk that he deals with joint irritation and inflammation, soft tissue injuries such as hamstring strains due to compensation or in attempts to stabilize his knee, or other compensatory injuries.

Notably, the Rams were rumored to be interested in Brown but backed out after reviewing his knee medicals. Knowing the tier of medical resources that the Rams have with Cedars-Sinai makes me lean towards avoiding Brown, but if he winds up making it through all of 2026 without issue, then I will certainly regret not picking him at cost.

For redraft, I am more inclined to invest, while in dynasty I would rather be a year early than a year late on pivoting to other options. The landing spot and current hype create a great opportunity to sell at a very nice price tag in dynasty.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: I wish I had a crystal ball to know exactly when Brown’s knee becomes a problem for his production. For dynasty, I would prefer to be out a year early than a year late. Despite this being a fantastic pivot in the situation from the Eagles pass attack to the Patriots pass attack, this is also the most value Brown may hold for a while, which makes selling tempting now rather than later. Regardless, he should pay off for contenders as long as the knee does not act up.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ I agree with Jeff here. Not changing Brown’s redraft ranking, but perhaps a player I want to sell-high on today or in October in my dynasty leagues.

__What’s your level of confidence in Quinshon Judkins heading into 2026?__

From an injury perspective, I have a high level of confidence in Quinshon Judkins despite it being his first year out from his injury. He suffered a fibular fracture with ankle dislocation with very minimal ligament damage and was cutting aggressively in OTAs. I do believe he will be very close to 100% for Week 1 and will likely be relied upon as the workhorse behind a bad offensive line and bad quarterback play.

My confidence is sky-high regarding his return-from-injury performance, but my concern is more about his offensive situation than anything else.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Draft Judkins despite returning from ankle dislocation and fracture, but beware of the Browns' offensive situation and their low points implied.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ Good news for Judkins drafters, but my concerns with Judkins have never been injury-related — they're more about his talent (and lack of pass-catching abilities), the offense, quarterback play, gamescript, the overall scoring environment, etc. He’s not really a player I’m all that excited to draft.

__Is Tetairoa McMillan much of an injury discount? He dealt with calf (Weeks 4-5), hamstring (Week 10), and a foot/ankle injury__ [__for much of the second half__](https://x.com/DaShawnWSOC9/status/2001414106763395457?s=20) __of the season, as well as an illness in Week 17, which led to his worst performance of the season.__

It appears that McMillan is currently going in the WR14-18 range, so I am not sure there is much of an injury discount. I find it difficult to choose McMillan ahead of any of the wide receivers chosen before him in drafts, especially given that he is already dealing with foot soreness after gaining weight (generally not a good thing, yet receivers still love to do this) and is receiving targets from Bryce Young.

Specific to the foot injury, he notably had a [left foot injury](https://x.com/jmthrivept/status/2065162510714687781?s=20) in 2024, an unspecified fracture that required surgery, and he dealt with an unspecified foot injury late in the 2025 season. Unfortunately, we do not know which foot was injured in 2025 or which foot he was dealing with soreness on this off-season, but it would make sense if it was the same side. If it is simply the hardware causing him some discomfort, he can play through it without much concern, but we unfortunately do not have any more details.

I do not mind picking him at cost and am not overly concerned about the injuries, but I would not view him as an injury discount at this time.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Be aware of the foot injury and past history since 2024, but since we do not know whether it is all left-sided, I would not hard-fade him at the current cost. I personally prefer other players in his range, but if you are in on McMillan for 2026, then I would not be overly concerned about the injury history at this current time.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ I love McMillan. I think he’s already a top-12 WR in the league, and had an even more impressive rookie season than he gets credit for — given all the injuries and how bad the QB play was. That said, he’s not a player I’m all that excited to draft, because I think the QB stinks.

__How many games is J.K. Dobbins going to miss this year?__

Is JK Dobbins injury-prone or simply the most unlucky running back of this decade? Possibly a little bit of both, but I do believe his most recent foot injury was incredibly unlucky while being tackled from behind and rolled up. I am still not 100% certain that he had a true Lisfranc repair, as those often come with close to a nine-month recovery, and he was cleared to practice within three months of surgery.

He has promised the media and fans that he will play all 17 games this year; a reasonable projection would be to expect Dobbins to play close to 13 games and value him accordingly, leaving room for excitement if he does play all 17.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: How much upside is there with a pure rusher with low receiving utilization, extensive past injury history whether unlucky or injury prone, and contending with two other running backs lurking in the shadows for workload? While I do believe Dobbins can actually stay healthy for the 2026 season and that his 2025 injury was extremely unlucky, I am completely fine avoiding him in drafts at the cost of other, higher-upside options in his range.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ Believe it or not, J.K. Dobbins was top-5 in rushing yards when he went down with a season-ending injury in Week 10. He’s not a terrible pick at his current ADP, but I agree with Jeff that there are better high-upside options in his draft range that I prefer.

__No concerns with Jonathon Brooks, correct? Should we be expecting the healthy 2023 version?__

I wouldn’t say “*no concerns*,” but I laid out some[](https://x.com/jmthrivept/status/2055743129408704806?s=20)[very good details](https://x.com/jmthrivept/status/2055743129408704806?s=20) about why I am acquiring him at cost after finding details about his second ACLR that should provide significant joint stability and reduce reinjury risk moving forward. He was looking explosive in OTAs, so hopefully that carries over into training camp, because the Panthers have continued to state their hopes of getting Brooks involved in the run game and especially the screen game, a key part of the offense that Dave Canales has been hoping to ignite over the past few years.

I anticipate a slow, cautious start for Brooks' utilization over the first quarter of the season, with a very good chance of increasing to a near 50/50 split or even taking over the majority of the backfield workload by midseason.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: I enjoyed acquiring Jonathon Brooks for future 3rds in dynasty leagues while I could, but thankfully his cost still accounts for the risk, while baking in the potential for him to earn more workload by midseason and possibly take over the majority of the backfield from Chuba Hubbard. I firmly believe the second ACL surgery fixed an issue with the graft from the first ACL surgery, and the team has been very cautious with his ramp-up. I am investing.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ Brooks is going to be one of my most-drafted RBs this year. If Jeff's optimism proves correct, he has legitimate league-winning upside at an RB39-44 price tag. And those are exactly the kinds of bets we want to make at that point in our drafts.

__When does Patrick Mahomes return to 100%? Does he play Week 1? We should expect a big dropoff in rushing, correct?__

Let me start off by reiterating that Patrick Mahomes is truly in the “freak athlete” tier in terms of injury return, alongside guys like Drew Brees, Tom Brady, George Kittle, and many other incredibly high-work-ethic players. On paper, from a tissue-healing perspective, I feel like I cannot say Mahomes will be 100% until November, but given that he is working relentlessly every single day, I do believe he will be very close to 100% production-wise by Week 1.

I would anticipate a drop-off in rushing production only due to fewer schemed rushing play calls and the addition of Kenneth Walker, but if he is on the field and a play breaks down into a potential scramble and rush attempt, he will not hesitate to take off and slide.

 Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes admits he carried the ball too much in 2025: "I think I ran a little bit too much last season... If all else fails, I'll just hand it off to K9 and let him go to work." — Charles Goldman (@goldmctNFL) July 24, 2026 

Point being, I am not fading Mahomes for 2026, especially now that Matt Nagy is gone, and you should not be fading him either. While he may have close to a 20% rushing dip in the first quarter to half of the season, I expect his passing production to make up for the deficit.

__Jeff’s TLDR__: Anticipate slight rushing production regression in the first quarter of the season, but I do expect a positive increase in passing production with Eric Bieniemy calling plays again and a likely lean on getting the ball out quickly to his playmakers. Do not fade Mahomes.

__Scott’s Takeaway:__ Sorry Jeff! I’ll be fading Mahomes at his current QB12 ADP. Brock Purdy averages more FPG over the last three seasons and is significantly cheaper. But I’d rather target a QB with more upside than Purdy or Mahomes anyway.
